clue.text: A mere puppet of Stravinsky

parts.note: the straw puppet who comes to life and gets his own ballet by Stravinsky (1911), the title role

explanation.surface: Someone dismissed as nothing more than the composer's creature.
explanation.definitionFit: The title character of Stravinsky's 1911 ballet is literally a puppet brought to life at a Russian fair.

clue.text: Big departure for second book

definitions.meaning: a mass leaving of people from a place
the second book of the Bible, after Genesis

explanation.surface: A grand farewell marks a writer's follow-up volume.
explanation.definitionFit: A mass emigration is called by this name, which is also the title of the Old Testament's second book, telling of the Israelites leaving Egypt.

clue.text: "For — he could not ope / His mouth but out there flew a trope" (Samuel Butler)

definitions.text: "For — he could not ope / His mouth but out there flew a trope" (Samuel Butler)

parts.words: "For — he could not ope / His mouth but out there flew a trope" (Samuel Butler)
parts.note: a couplet from Butler's mock-epic Hudibras with the missing word, the art of persuasive speech, to be supplied

explanation.surface: A quotation from Hudibras about a man who cannot speak without figures of speech.
explanation.definitionFit: Tropes are figures of speech, the stock-in-trade of the art of eloquent persuasion, which is the word Butler wrote in the gap.

clue.text: Don DelLillo's nether regions

definitions.meaning: Don DeLillo's 1997 novel, the spelling of his name as printed here
the realm below, Hades or the criminal world

explanation.surface: An American novelist's work dwells on the lower depths.
explanation.definitionFit: DeLillo's big novel of 1997 bears this title, which also names Hades, the realm beneath the earth.

clue.text: Surrey's the end of E. M. Forster

definitions.text: Surrey's the end of E. M. Forster

parts.words: Surrey's the end of E. M. Forster
parts.note: Henry Howard, Earl of Surrey, was a Tudor poet, so Surrey's is his family's; Forster's novel title adds the word End

explanation.surface: The county seems to have finished off the novelist.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'Surrey's' as the poet Earl of Surrey's family name with a possessive, and 'the end' as the word End completing Forster's 1910 novel title.
explanation.definitionFit: Forster's novel is named after a house, and the family name of the Earl of Surrey supplies its first word, so the plural is wanted.

clue.text: Old wool ship

parts.note: the ancient vessel of Jason that sailed in quest of the Golden Fleece

explanation.surface: A vintage vessel for carrying fleeces to market.
explanation.definitionFit: Jason and his crew sailed this legendary ship to fetch the Golden Fleece, so it was literally after wool.

clue.text: Dad, Greek publisher of contemporary musicians?

parts.note: pop is an informal word for father
OUP is Oxford University Press, the publisher

explanation.surface: A father, a Greek and a publisher are listed as some modern band members.
explanation.definitionFit: A band playing modern chart music is the usual sense; the question mark admits it is a loose gloss.

clue.text: My class act farce or disasters

indicators.note: a farce is chaotic comedy, so the three words are thrown into disorder

explanation.surface: Someone describes their own stage performance as either a farce or a string of disasters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'farce' looks like part of the self-deprecating surface but tells you to rearrange MY CLASS ACT.
explanation.definitionFit: Upheavals and catastrophes of great violence are both meanings; the word is a stronger synonym for calamities.

clue.text: Florentine heroine with zero pounds in capital

indicators.note: the zero and pounds sit inside the name of the capital

parts.note: Roma is the Italian name of Rome, Italy's capital
a zero looks like the letter O
L is the abbreviation for pounds, from Latin libra

explanation.surface: A Florentine woman arrives penniless in the capital.
explanation.walkthrough: The title heroine of George Eliot's novel set in Renaissance Florence.
explanation.definitionFit: George Eliot's 1863 novel is named after its heroine, the daughter of a Florentine scholar.

clue.text: Walk three times round one who has eaten it, Coleridge suggests

definitions.text: Walk three times round one who has eaten it, Coleridge suggests

parts.words: Walk three times round one who has eaten it, Coleridge suggests
parts.note: Kubla Khan ends 'Weave a circle round him thrice ... For he on --- hath fed', the food of paradise

explanation.surface: Coleridge recommends a ritual to perform around someone who has eaten a certain thing.
explanation.definitionFit: In Kubla Khan the inspired poet has fed on this paradisal sweet substance, so onlookers must circle him three times.

clue.text: The cardinal wrote one for his life

definitions.text: The cardinal wrote one for his life

parts.words: The cardinal wrote one for his life
parts.note: Cardinal Newman's 1864 defence of his religious life was titled with a Latin phrase meaning a defence 'for his life'

explanation.surface: A churchman composes something on behalf of his own life.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for his life' translates 'pro vita sua', the rest of Newman's title.
explanation.definitionFit: A formal written defence of one's opinions or conduct; Newman's famous one justified his conversion.

clue.text: Emperor returns to lead Rastafarians

indicators.note: the leading letters are read backwards, coming back the other way
the letters wanted are the ones at the front of the word Rastafarians

explanation.surface: An emperor comes back to head a Rastafarian community.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to lead' picks RAST from the front of Rastafarians, and 'returns' reads it backwards. Fittingly, the movement takes its name from Ras Tafari, the emperor Haile Selassie.
explanation.definitionFit: The Russian imperial ruler's title comes from Caesar, so he was an emperor.

clue.text: Du Maurier's out-of-this-world character chronicled by Bradbury

definitions.text: Du Maurier's out-of-this-world character chronicled by Bradbury

parts.words: Du Maurier's out-of-this-world character chronicled by Bradbury
parts.note: George du Maurier's last novel (1897) has this title, and Ray Bradbury's stories of Mars are its Chronicles

explanation.surface: A Du Maurier character from another planet is written up by Bradbury.
explanation.walkthrough: The Du Maurier is George, author of Trilby, not his granddaughter Daphne.
explanation.definitionFit: Both writers' titles name a native of the red planet, an out-of-this-world figure in the literal sense.

clue.text: Powellian figure, primed perhaps, in cashmere

indicators.note: the rearranged letters sit inside the fabric word

parts.note: cashmere is a kind of wool

indicators.note: perhaps shows the letters of primed are only one possible arrangement

explanation.surface: A character from Powell's novels, possibly made up, wears cashmere.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Powellian figure' points to Kenneth Widmerpool, the ambitious bore of Anthony Powell's A Dance to the Music of Time; 'primed' is the fodder, not a description of him.
explanation.definitionFit: Anthony Powell's best-known creation, the pushy careerist of his twelve-novel sequence, is this figure.

clue.text: Mouldy, not fit for it, thought Falstaff

definitions.text: Mouldy, not fit for it, thought Falstaff

parts.words: Mouldy, not fit for it, thought Falstaff
parts.note: in Henry IV Part 2 Falstaff inspects recruits including Ralph Mouldy, who buys his way out of being taken for the army

explanation.surface: Falstaff judges a stale thing unsuitable.
explanation.walkthrough: Mouldy is a character's name, not decay: one of the country recruits Falstaff musters in Gloucestershire.
explanation.definitionFit: Joining up as a soldier is what Mouldy was judged unfit for when Falstaff picked recruits.

clue.text: Choose academician for classic tragedy

parts.note: to elect is to choose by vote
RA is a Royal Academician, a member of the Royal Academy of Arts

explanation.surface: Picking a member of the Academy for a role in a great Greek play.
explanation.definitionFit: Sophocles and Euripides each wrote a Greek tragedy named after Agamemnon's vengeful daughter.

clue.text: Warner's prank

definitions.meaning: Rex Warner's 1953 novel has this one-word title

explanation.surface: A trick played by someone named Warner.
explanation.definitionFit: Rex Warner gave a novel this title, and the word also means a reckless mischievous adventure.

clue.text: Where the gods might provide a fine view of the stage below

definitions.text: Where the gods might provide a fine view of the stage below

parts.words: Where the gods might provide a fine view of the stage below
parts.note: the gods are both the Greek deities and the highest theatre gallery; the deities' mountain home looks down on the world's stage

explanation.surface: A theatregoer praises the cheap seats high up for their view of the stage.
explanation.walkthrough: In British theatres 'the gods' is the top gallery; here the gods are the Greek pantheon and the stage is the world below their mountain.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek gods lived on this mountain, from which they looked down on mortal affairs.

clue.text: We may share his disenchantment

parts.note: C. E. ... 1922 book Disenchantment recorded the disillusion of soldiers in the Great War

explanation.surface: We might feel the same disillusion as some man.
explanation.walkthrough: Disenchantment is a book title here, not a feeling: the classic memoir of disillusion after the First World War.
explanation.definitionFit: C. E. Montague, the journalist, wrote Disenchantment, so this surname belongs to its author.

clue.text: "If living isn't a seeking for the grail, it may be a damned game" (Scott Fitzgerald)

definitions.text: "If living isn't a seeking for the grail, it may be a damned game" (Scott Fitzgerald)

parts.words: "If living isn't a seeking for the grail, it may be a damned game" (Scott Fitzgerald)
parts.note: the line from This Side of Paradise has the gap before 'game', an adjective meaning entertaining

explanation.surface: A Fitzgerald quotation about life as a quest or a game.
explanation.definitionFit: Fitzgerald's adjective means entertaining or diverting, the consolation if life is no holy quest.

clue.text: Chair Dumas recreated for Spartan king

indicators.note: recreated means made anew, so the letters of the two words are rebuilt in a fresh order

explanation.surface: A piece of furniture and a French novelist are reworked into a Spartan monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: Five Spartan kings bore the name; Shakespeare also uses it for a Bohemian lord in The Winter's Tale.
explanation.definitionFit: Several kings of ancient Sparta, including the ruler at the start of the Peloponnesian War, had this name.

clue.text: We French at home in Nichols piece

definitions.text: We French at home in Nichols piece

parts.words: We French at home in Nichols piece
parts.note: French for 'we' is also the second word of Peter Nichols's 1974 play whose title means 'at our home'

explanation.surface: French speakers feel at home in a work by Nichols.
explanation.walkthrough: The play is Chez Nous; 'at home' gives chez, and the gap after it is filled by the French pronoun.
explanation.definitionFit: The French first-person plural pronoun completes the title of the Nichols play, Chez ---, 'at our place'.

clue.text: Sign of sound change by German writer

definitions.text: Sign of sound change by German writer

parts.words: Sign of sound change by German writer
parts.note: the two dots a German writer puts over a vowel show its sound has shifted; the German word combines 'around' and 'sound'

explanation.surface: Some token of a shift in tone by a German author.
explanation.walkthrough: 'German writer' seems to be an author, but it is anyone writing German, who marks a changed vowel with two dots.
explanation.definitionFit: The diacritic of two dots over a vowel marks a vowel shift in German, as in Mädchen or schön.

clue.text: Leading ladies in Churchill play?

parts.note: Caryl Churchill's 1982 play about successful women; leading ladies can be read as women at the top

explanation.surface: The stars of a play somehow connected to Churchill.
explanation.walkthrough: Churchill here is the playwright Caryl Churchill, not Winston.
explanation.definitionFit: Caryl Churchill's play gathers high-achieving women, the leading ladies of its title.

clue.text: Poet laureate, some hero we acknowledge

indicators.note: some means only a part of the words hero we is taken

explanation.surface: We salute a fragment of hero worship for a laureate.
explanation.walkthrough: Nicholas Rowe, playwright and editor of Shakespeare, was Poet Laureate from 1715.
explanation.definitionFit: Nicholas Rowe held the post of Poet Laureate from 1715 until his death in 1718.

clue.text: Go admire sort of symbol

indicators.note: sort of means a version of, so the letters of go admire are rearranged

explanation.surface: An invitation to go and admire some kind of symbol.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sort of' looks like it qualifies 'symbol' but tells you to rearrange GO ADMIRE.
explanation.definitionFit: A written character standing for an idea, as in Chinese script, is a kind of symbol.

clue.text: Prior's merry jester

parts.note: Matthew Prior's poetry features the phrase, and prior also suggests a monk

explanation.surface: A monastery's head keeps a cheerful clown.
explanation.walkthrough: Prior is the poet Matthew Prior, not a monk; 'merry' plus this name makes the old word for a clown.
explanation.definitionFit: A buffoon or clown was called a merry andrew, so this name follows 'merry' for a jester.

clue.text: Date for an April ride, Longfellow recalls

definitions.text: Date for an April ride, Longfellow recalls

parts.words: Date for an April ride, Longfellow recalls
parts.note: Paul Revere's Ride begins with his midnight ride on a day in April 1775, given as 'the --- of April, in Seventy-five'

explanation.surface: Longfellow remembers when a spring ride took place.
explanation.definitionFit: Longfellow's poem dates Paul Revere's ride to the day after the seventeenth of April, 1775.
